full_text: Vànuatu Special Envoy calls for Pacific to access West Papua. The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) should revisit a proposal for an independent regional delegation to visit West Papua and assess reported human rights concerns, Vanuatu Special Envoy on Decolonisation and Maritime Boundaries Delimitation Joe Natuman says. With the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting (PIFLM) approaching, Natuman said Pacific leaders have an opportunity to reconsider the issue and determine how the region can respond to continuing concerns about human rights and the wellbeing of the people of West Papua. Natuman, a former Prime Minister, said the Forum had previously proposed sending a delegation to West Papua to assess the human rights situation directly. However, he said the Forum had written to the Indonesian Government regarding the proposed visit but had not received a response. He said direct access remains important if Pacific leaders are to develop a clearer understanding of the situation and consider reports of human rights concerns raised at regional and international levels. The proposed visit could provide a fact-finding mechanism for Pacific countries, allowing representatives to engage with relevant stakeholders and assess conditions before reporting their findings to the Forum. Natuman said the issue also extends to the participation of West Papuan representatives in regional and international forums, where he claimed their involvement has faced obstacles. He pointed to similar challenges within the Melanesian Spearhead Group and said there would be no West Papuan delegation attending the upcoming PIF. Natuman also referred to discussions surrounding West Papua at United Nations human rights mechanisms in Geneva, arguing that Indonesia’s position within international institutions has presented additional challenges for those seeking greater access to the territory. With the Forum meeting approaching, Natuman said Pacific leaders should reconsider West Papua

full_text: MSG LEADERS' RESOLUTION PRESENTED TO THE UN HUMAN RIGHTS COUNCIL The Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG) Secretariat formally presented the Pacific and MSG Leaders' resolution for the Human Rights Commission to visit West Papua and the Papuan Provinces in Indonesia during the 19th session of the Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (EMRIP) in Geneva, Switzerland. EMRIP is a key advisory body of the UN Human Rights Council. Its role is to provide critical advice to the Human Rights Council on the implementation of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). The activity was actioned in line with the Leaders' Mandate. During the 22nd MSG Leaders’ Summit held in Port Vila in June 2023, MSG Leaders supported the call made by Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders in 2019 for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to visit West Papua and the Papuan Provinces. The call was reiterated by Pacific Leaders in 2025 during the PIF Leaders' meeting in Honiara and the MSG Summit in Suva, Fiji. The Acting Director General (ADG), Mr. Ilan Kiloe, said the MSG Secretariat’s engagement with the UN Human Rights Mechanisms is an important step in advancing the PIF and MSG Leaders' decision. “It is a small but significant step towards the implementation of the leaders’ decision to advance the voices of Melanesian peoples on the international stage and demonstrates the organization's strong commitment to promoting justice, human rights, and the rights of Indigenous Peoples,” Mr. Kiloe said. "The MSG Secretariat has championed advocacy on indigenous rights during the recently concluded ICJ Advisory Opinion on the obligations of states in respect to Climate Change, and we must continue to demonstrate that commitment," he added. In addition to attending the EMRIP session, the MSG Secretariat held a number of targeted bilateral meetings, particularly with the Chairperson of the Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (EMRIP), Ms. Valmaine Toki; the Special Rapporteur on Indigenous Peoples, Dr. Albert K. Barume; the Chief of the Indigenous Peoples & Minorities Section of the United Nations, Mr. Hernan Vales; and special representatives of the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), UN Treaty Bodies, the UN Voluntary Fund, and the UN Youth Office. The mission concluded with a formal briefing session with the MSG Ambassadors & Permanent Representatives to the United Nations (PRUNs) based in Geneva, Switzerland. The briefing was organized by the Vanuatu Ambassador to the UN in Geneva, H.E. Sylvain Kalsakau, and hosted by Ambassador Mere Falemaka in the PIF Permanent Mission conference room. The MSG Secretariat team was led by ADG Kiloe and supported by Political Affairs Officer Richard Balkonan and Acting Programme Manager/Legal Officer Brittien Yosef. 📍 Photo: Acting Director General Ilan Kiloe, MSG Secretariat team, and MSG Ambassadors during the Geneva briefing hosted at the PIF Permanent Mission. #MSGSecretariat #Melanesia #HumanRights #IndigenousRights #EMRIP19 #Geneva #PacificIslands @followers

full_text: The Pacific Conference of Churches continues to affirm its commitment to advocate and inspire actions in solidarity for the United Liberation Movement of West Papua (ULMWP) to become a full member of Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG). This morning, the PCC hosted Civil Society partners alongside the ULMWP President Benny Wenda at a prayer vigil where the Morning Star flag was raised in Suva, ahead of the MSG Leaders’ Summit in Vanuatu next week. Mr Wenda presented the PCC General Secretary, Reverend James Bhagwan, with a new flag that symbolises hope and unity despite Indonesia’s blatant violations of West Papuans’ human rights. Reverend Bhagwan said it was significant to gesture linking the churches and people of the Pacific to focus their attention on the struggle of our sisters and brothers in Tanah Papua. “PCC have been flying the Morning Star flag even though it was in tatters to remind us that while our family/vuvale in Papua are oppressed, displaced, repressed and face constant attacks on their dignity and human rights, they remain hopeful for their right to be self-determining,” Revered Bhagwan shared. He said the new flag will continue to fly everyday as a sign of hope and reminder that the Pacific family is rallying behind the people of West Papua. “You do not go alone to that MSG meeting, you go with God and with us in your heart, knowing that while you await formal recognition of ULMWP as a full member of the Melanesian Spearhead Group, your Pacific Churches and Civil Society, the people of the Pacific have recognised the ULMWP as the political representative of the people of Tanah Papua,” he added. PCC alongside our partners will continue to engage in peaceful actions this week as we our support the call of the ULMWP and Government of Vanuatu to bring West Papua back to the MSG family by granting ULMWP full membership to the MSG and acknowledging the ULMWP as the main political representative of the people of West Papua. 12-07-2023 Ends.

full_text: I’M A PAPUA NEW GUINEAN WHO SUPPORTS PRESIDENT TRUMP AND MAGA. This November will mark almost 3 years since I got on this train. During that time, I’ve gotten off at the station two or three times to reset, deal with personal responsibilities, focus on my family and handle life thousands of miles away in Papua New Guinea. But I have NEVER gotten off the train itself. Not once. And there’s a reason for that. Before I publicly supported President Trump and MAGA, I spent time trying to understand what I was actually supporting. I studied the vision. I studied the agenda. I looked at America’s position in the world. I looked at the economy, energy, borders, trade, national security, foreign policy, culture, family and the direction Western civilization was heading. I also understood something many people seem to forget: AMERICA FIRST means AMERICA FIRST. I’m not an American. I live thousands of miles across the Pacific Ocean in Papua New Guinea. So I understood from the beginning that policies designed primarily to benefit Americans could sometimes create consequences for countries like mine. And they have. Some decisions made in Washington eventually reach people on the other side of the Pacific. I have felt some of those consequences personally. My family has felt them. Businesses feel them. Countries feel them. But I never expected the President of the United States to put Papua New Guinea first. His responsibility is to put America first. That is literally the job Americans elected him to do. At the same time, I believe a stronger, more stable and more prosperous America ultimately matters enormously to the rest of the world. That is why I don’t judge every policy based purely on whether it makes my own life easier this month. I look at the bigger picture. I look at where America is trying to go. I look at what kind of world my children are going to inherit. I have six kids. And as a father, there are certain principles I’m simply not prepared to casually surrender: God. Family. Freedom. Secure borders. Law and order. Parental responsibility. Free speech. Religious liberty. Personal responsibility. National sovereignty. Strong communities. Opportunity. The dignity of work. Peace through strength. You don’t have to agree with me on every policy. You don’t even have to like President Trump personally. But Americans should understand something incredibly important before the midterms: A President cannot govern in a vacuum. The people Americans send to Congress matter. The Senate matters. The House matters. Governors matter. State legislatures matter. Local elections matter. Every major political vision eventually runs into the reality of votes, legislation, budgets, confirmations, courts, bureaucracy and institutional resistance. That means sitting at home because you’re disappointed about one issue can eventually help determine the outcome of ten other issues you care deeply about. If I lived in America right now, I already know what I would be doing. I’d be knocking on doors. I’d be talking to voters. I’d be helping with communications. I’d be helping with strategy and PR, because those are areas where I know I can contribute. I’d be explaining policy. I’d be encouraging people to research candidates. I’d be reminding Americans that elections have consequences long after Election Day. But I’m not in America. I’m in Papua New Guinea. So the least I can do is use the platform I have. That’s what I’ve been doing since I had 9 followers on X. Nine. I didn’t start talking about these issues after building an audience. I built an audience while talking about them. And here I am years later, still trying to educate people the best way I know how. Sometimes I’ll get things wrong. Sometimes people will disagree with me. Sometimes policies I support will indirectly make life harder for me personally. That comes with thinking seriously about politics instead of treating politics like a football match. My support was never supposed to mean: “Everything will be perfect.” It means I looked at the competing visions for America and decided which direction I believe gives America - and ultimately the free world - the strongest future. And I’m still standing there. The next few months matter. If you’re an American reading this, don’t outsource your political thinking to a 30-second video. Don’t base your vote on one headline. Don’t assume somebody else will show up. Study the policies. Study the candidates. Study the direction of the country. Understand what is actually at stake. Then VOTE. Because whether America becomes stronger during President Trump’s term will not depend on one man sitting inside the White House. It will also depend on whether millions of ordinary Americans understand the power of the ballot sitting in their own hands. 🇺🇸

full_text: “RSS Out of NYC”, “Hindutva Out of NYC” and “India Belongs to Everyone” were among the slogans raised by protesters outside Madison Square Garden in New York on August 29, as RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed a major gathering of Indian-American and interfaith groups. The protest was organised by Hindus for Human Rights and allied organisations, with Muslim, Sikh and Christian groups and other advocacy organisations also participating. Bhagwat’s New York visit included two separate events. Earlier on August 29, he participated in the “One World, One Humanity” Faith Leaders’ Conference, which brought together religious leaders from Hinduism, Islam, Christianity and Judaism for discussions centred on interfaith dialogue, unity and shared humanity. Later, he was the keynote speaker at the “Universal Oneness Celebration” at Madison Square Garden, organised by the American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD) Forum. The event was presented by organisers as a celebration of Hindu philosophy, diversity, interfaith harmony and the principle of “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam” – the world as one family. Around 5,000 people were expected to attend. At the Faith Leaders’ Conference, Bhagwat said: “If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslim in Bharat, he will not remain Hindu.” He also spoke about the idea that different faiths may follow different paths while sharing a common humanity. His appearance at MSG, however, drew significant opposition in New York, including from 61 organisations that said the RSS does not represent their vision of Hinduism or India.

full_text: THERE IS A PART OF PAPUA NEW GUINEA WHERE THE RIVER IS NOT SOMETHING YOU VISIT. THE RIVER IS THE ROAD. 🇵🇬 Welcome to the Sepik River system. The Sepik stretches for more than 1,100 kilometres through northern New Guinea. Its basin covers roughly 77,000–80,000 square kilometres. That's an area larger than several entire countries. But the numbers don't really explain it. Imagine a world of: - Rivers. - Tributaries. - Swamps. - Oxbow lakes. - Floodplains. - Villages. - Canoes. - Forest. And communities whose movement, food, culture and relationships have been shaped by water for generations. Some research describes the Sepik basin as one of the largest and most intact freshwater systems in the Asia-Pacific. Its floodplain alone contains huge numbers of lakes, including around 1,500 oxbow and associated lakes according to PNG water-resource documentation. And here's the part an American might appreciate. Think about the Mississippi River. It helped shape cities, commerce, culture, music, agriculture and settlement across America. Now imagine a river system where large stretches remain far less industrialized... where communities still rely heavily on canoes... and where traditional art, architecture and cultural identity remain deeply connected to the river itself. That's the Sepik. Not an American Mississippi. Not an Amazon imitation. Its own civilization shaped around water. And getting there is exactly why PNG isn't ordinary tourism. You're not necessarily landing at an airport, renting a car and following Interstate signs. In some places... the river becomes your highway. You travel by boat. You stop at villages. You move through landscapes with very little resemblance to your everyday life back home. That is precisely the kind of travel experience that is becoming increasingly rare. The world has become extraordinarily connected. You can find McDonald's in dozens of countries. Same smartphones. Same clothing brands. Same hotel chains. Same social media. But there are still places where geography strongly dictates how people live. The Sepik is one of them. And one day, I'd like HausLink to make journeys into places like this far easier for international travellers to discover and coordinate... without destroying the very thing that makes them extraordinary. PNG should never compete by becoming more ordinary. Our advantage is that parts of this country are anything BUT ordinary. 🇵🇬

full_text: State Department Revokes Visa Of Iraqi National On FBI Terror Watchlist | Kimberly Hayek, The Epoch Times The State Department has revoked the visa of an Iraqi national who was placed on the FBI's Terror Watchlist, ending her ability to enter the United States years after she received a high-profile award from the Biden administration. Taif Sami Mohammed Al Shakarchi is no longer present in the United States, according to a statement released Friday by Assistant Secretary Dylan Johnson. The revocation followed her placement on the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Terror Watchlist. No further details on the underlying intelligence were provided in the department's announcement. "Under President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, suspected terrorists will never be allowed to remain in the United States," the statement read. Al Shakarchi was given the International Woman of Courage Award in 2022 by then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken and then-First Lady Jill Biden. The department said she had been recognized for her purported role in fighting corruption and her advocacy for "gender equity." The award recognized "women from around the globe who have demonstrated exceptional courage, strength, and leadership in advocating for peace, justice, human rights, gender equity and equality, and the empowerment of women and girls, in all their diversity." Al Shakarchi, also referred to in State Department materials as Taif Sami Mohammed, had served as Iraq's deputy finance minister. She was described at the time of the 2022 award as a longtime official in the Ministry of Finance who started out as a budget analyst in 1985 and rose to director general of the Budget Department. Officials then called her a front-line leader against corrupt practices and noted she was known as the "Iron Woman." She was listed as a political independent. The 2022 ceremony, held virtually, was hosted by Blinken with Jill Biden delivering remarks. Twelve women from various countries received the honor that year. The Trump administration has made clear it prioritizes removing individuals it views as security risks. In recent months, the State Department has revoked hundreds of visas in targeted efforts, including nearly 900 people targeted by a birth tourism task force launched in early August. Broader continuous-vetting operations have led to more than 175,000 visa revocations for a range of violations, crimes, and national security concerns. The International Women of Courage Award itself continues under the Trump administration. First lady Melania Trump and Rubio presented the 2025 honors in April, recognizing women from countries including Burkina Faso, Israel, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Romania, South Sudan, Sri Lanka, and Yemen. The department has noted that more than 200 women from over 90 countries have received the award since it began in 2007. Al Shakarchi's case stands apart due to the later watchlist designation. The State Department says its visa action is a straightforward application of its policy against allowing suspected terrorists to stay. The department's release did not specify where she is now or provide additional biographical updates beyond the watchlist status and her departure from the United States. Visa decisions rest with the executive branch, with courts offering limited recourse to many such revocations, a principle reinforced in prior Supreme Court rulings on related immigration matters. The move arrives amid wider efforts by the administration to tighten scrutiny of foreign nationals already inside the country or seeking entry. Officials tie those steps to national security priorities under the Trump administration. https://t.co/fjpEONdW16

full_text: Reimagining World Wrestling Entertainment World Wrestling Entertainment needs a complete reset: not less wrestling, but a stronger identity built around professional wrestling as a major sporting institution. The model would combine modern production and competitive structure with the principles of Jesse McMahon, Vince J. McMahon Sr. and Toots Mondt: strong local markets, memorable attractions, dependable touring and the ring at the center of the business. The WWE brand would remain, but the current television ecosystem would end. There would be one unified roster with no brand split, rotating between Monday and Friday broadcasts according to rankings, rivalries and schedules. No Raw. No SmackDown. Just World Wrestling Entertainment. Madison Square Garden would be WWE’s home turf, serving as its symbolic headquarters, much as Arena México does for CMLL and the Tokyo Dome for NJPW. It would host major title defenses, tournament finals, landmark debuts and historic rivalries. WWE would tour nationally and internationally, but MSG would remain its defining venue. Following the McMahon tradition, WWE would cultivate regional relationships rather than merely visit cities. Arenas, promoters, wrestling schools and fan communities would become part of a dependable national touring network. The presentation would be stripped down. Replace the entrance stage with a simple entrance tunnel leading directly to the ring. Television would combine house-show intimacy, boxing and MMA intensity, and independent-wrestling grit: fewer cuts, minimal graphics, natural crowd noise and limited CGI. Blood and profanity would be used sparingly, when they add genuine intensity. Inspired by Mondt, WWE would emphasize clear stakes, strong finishes and wrestlers capable of carrying a card. Matches would have time limits, rankings and official records. Referees would function like boxing or MMA officials, with authority to enforce rules, stop matches and protect competitors. Outside interference would be prohibited and severely punished. Championships would resemble prestigious sporting trophies, not oversized corporate props. Tag-team and women’s wrestling would be major attractions, with their own rankings, records, tournaments and championship programs. Either division could headline a broadcast or major event. The annual calendar would center on Royal Rumble, WrestleMania and SummerSlam, supported by two major tournaments: The Wrestling Classic, a World Cup-style international competition, and King of the Ring, an open, FA Cup-style knockout tournament. Ohio Valley Wrestling would serve as WWE’s primary developmental system, retaining its identity while training wrestlers in fundamentals, conditioning, psychology, promos and WWE’s competitive rules. WWE should also learn from Game Changer Wrestling and Major League Wrestling. GCW offers lessons in intimacy, unpredictability and fan connection; MLW shows that “major league” does not require a polished or sanitized product. WWE should be professional, not sterile; major league, not corporate-looking. Commercialization would remain necessary but secondary. Fans should feel like members of a wrestling community, not targets of constant marketing. The goal is a distinct North American wrestling culture: sporting seriousness, cultural passion, strong markets, memorable attractions, disciplined touring and respect for the audience. One WWE. One roster. Madison Square Garden as home turf. Strong local markets. Meaningful competition. Prestigious championships. Serious officiating. Gritty presentation. Fewer distractions. More wrestling.

full_text: AMERICA JUST HOSTED THE BIGGEST FIFA WORLD CUP IN HISTORY. More than 6.8 million people packed stadiums across North America to watch countries bring their own style, identity and culture to the same game. But over in Papua New Guinea, there is another sporting story that is completely different. We took a British sport and basically turned it into our own cultural event. 🇵🇬 Welcome to Trobriand Cricket. Cricket was introduced to the Trobriand Islands more than a century ago. But the islanders didn't simply adopt the British version. They transformed it. The teams can be enormous. There can be chanting. Dancing. Taunting. Ceremonial entrances. Celebrations after dismissals. Traditional rivalry. And the whole event can become as much a social and cultural performance as a sporting contest. Anthropologists became so fascinated by it that a famous documentary was made about the game in the 1970s. Think about how interesting that is. A sport arrives from another part of the world... and instead of the local population simply copying it... they absorb it into their own culture until it becomes recognizably Papua New Guinean. That is PNG in a nutshell. Outside influences have reached this country for generations. - Missionaries. - Colonial governments. - War. - Trade. - Christianity. - Modern technology. - Globalization. But underneath all of that remain hundreds of distinct cultures that continuously adapt things in their own way. So imagine being an American who just spent a month watching the World Cup... then travelling halfway around the world and seeing what organized sport looks like in a remote island community in Papua New Guinea. Same human instinct: - Competition. - Pride. - Community. - Celebration. - Completely different expression. That's why travelling matters. Sometimes you don't travel halfway across the world to see something “better.” You travel to see something you could never have imagined from home. Oh and the beaches and islands around this part of PNG are spectacular. Cruise ships go there annually but you can register your interest via HausLink to travel here sometime in the future. This journey is EXTREMELY safe. From arrival to departure, you'll Transit through Port Moresby to Alotau and then to Trobriand Islands and back. 🇺🇸✈️🇵🇬

The ULMWP have been elevating the issues and concerns affecting West Papua at all levels and have been accumulating widespread recognition internationally. The ULMWP has been seeking political recognition at the regional sub-grouping, the Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG). Yet Indonesia was granted associate status to the MSG with no proper criteria, and ULMWP made an observer. full_text: SOMEWHERE ALONG THE SEPIK RIVER IN PAPUA NEW GUINEA, THERE ARE MEN WHO CARRY THE CROCODILE ON THEIR OWN SKIN. Not as a tattoo. As scars. 🇵🇬 In some Sepik cultures, the crocodile has profound spiritual and cultural significance. Traditional male initiation ceremonies have involved carefully cutting patterns into the skin. When healed, the raised scars resemble the scales or markings of a crocodile. The Metropolitan Museum of Art has documented similar traditions among Sepik peoples, where crocodile imagery is tied to initiation, power and transformation. To an outsider, the first reaction might simply be: “That looks painful.” Of course it is. But if that's all we see, we miss the point. For the people involved, traditions like these can carry meanings involving: - Identity. - Manhood. - Ancestry. - Community. - Spiritual belief. - Belonging. - Transformation. - Cultural continuity. And this is where travelling somewhere culturally different becomes valuable. You don't have to practice another person's tradition. You don't even have to understand it immediately. But travel puts you in situations where you're forced to realize something: Human beings have developed completely different ways of understanding life. That is especially true in Papua New Guinea. The Sepik alone contains art, architecture, stories and traditions unlike almost anywhere else on Earth. And I would strongly argue that if you ever visit these communities, you shouldn't go there expecting people to “perform” culture for you. Go respectfully. Use local guides. Ask before taking photographs. Listen. Learn. Spend money in the communities hosting you where you can. Then leave with a better understanding of a world you didn't know existed. That's the kind of tourism PNG should be building. Not mass tourism. Meaningful tourism. And if you're reading this from halfway across the world thinking: “I'd actually like to travel the Sepik River one day and experience these cultures and traditions for myself...” Good. That's exactly how the journey starts. 🇵🇬 I'm building HausLink to help make journeys like this into Papua New Guinea easier to discover, plan and eventually experience with the right local coordination. If enough people raise their hands, we'll know exactly where to start building the journeys. Other awesome destinations are in the works. full_text: Guerrilla fighters from the West Papua National Liberation Army (TPNPB) ambushed Indonesian military forces. The TPNPB is the armed wing of the Free Papua Movement, which seeks independence for West Papua from Indonesia. The Papua conflict is a low-intensity guerrilla war that has lasted since the 1960s, rooted in Dutch colonial rule. West Papua was formally colonized by the Netherlands in 1898. Dutch control in the region that makes up present-day Indonesia began as early as the 1600s through the Dutch East India Company. After gaining independence, Indonesia took control of West Papua and began exploiting its natural resources on behalf of foreign corporations. Estimates suggest that up to 500,000 people—mostly Indigenous Papuans—have been killed in the conflict. Despite spanning over 60 years, the war remains one of the least reported armed struggles in the world.

full_text: We did not invade Java. We did not invade Jakarta or any other part of Indonesia. West Papua is our homeland. No one should tell us that only powerful states have the right to defend their people, their culture, their lands or their future. The principles of self-determination and decolonization were not written for the powerful alone, they were written for all peoples. For more than 64 years, West Papuans have primarily pursued recognition through peaceful political advocacy. We have petitioned governments, engaged with the United Nations, spoken to the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, the United States, the Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG) and the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), calling for the implementation of our right to self-determination and for West Papua to be returned to the UN decolonization agenda. Our position is rooted in the belief that the people of West Papua are entitled to determine their own political future. We point to historical commitments made during the Dutch administration, including the preparation for self-government and statements made in 1961 affirming the principle that self-determination belongs to all peoples, including the people of West Papua. Meanwhile, generations of Papuans have endured conflict, displacement and profound social and environmental change. Reports from governments, NGOs and international organizations have documented decades of violence, internal displacement and the rapid transformation of Papuan lands, including large-scale development projects in Merauke. These realities continue to shape how many Papuans understand the conflict today. When European governments speak openly about investing billions to defend their sovereignty and security, few question that states have a responsibility to protect their people. Our question is simple: Why are the aspirations and security concerns of West Papuans so often viewed through a different lens? Whether people agree or disagree with our political position, our history deserves to be understood in its full context, not reduced to a single headline or a single incident. As International Spokesperson for the ULMWP, I will continue to advocate for the political aspirations of the West Papuan people and to argue that any discussion of this conflict must begin with its history, its human consequences, and the principle that all peoples deserve equal consideration under international law. Context matters. History matters. Human dignity matters. #FreeWestPapua #EndColonialism #SelfDetermination #HumanRights #ContextMatters

full_text: "The massive expansion in trade following the handover of Papua in 1905 demonstrates that Australia immediately began its extraterritorial imperialism in earnest—and pursued its imperial aggrandizing policy in the Western Pacific with far more vigor than the British ever mustered. Now imagine arriving here... and needing serious cold-weather clothing. 😅 🇵🇬 Welcome to Mount Wilhelm. At approximately 4,509 metres - 14,793 feet - above sea level, Mount Wilhelm is the highest mountain in Papua New Guinea. That is higher than almost every mountain in the continental United States outside Alaska. And yes... it gets COLD. The PNG Tourism Promotion Authority actually advises visitors to bring cold-weather gear and notes that the high mountains can occasionally experience snow. Now think about how strange PNG's geography is. You could begin your journey around tropical coastline... then travel into the Highlands... walk past gardens and mountain communities... climb through increasingly cold terrain... and eventually stand on the highest point in the country. From the summit on a clear day, you're looking across one of the most rugged landscapes in the Pacific. This is something people constantly underestimate about PNG. We don't have one landscape. We have: - Coral islands. - Mangroves. - Savannah. - Rainforest. - River systems. - Volcanic landscapes. - Massive valleys. - And mountains exceeding 14,000 feet. All inside one country sitting just south of the equator. So here's another item for the bucket list: "Climb the highest mountain in Papua New Guinea." And perhaps enjoy telling your friends afterward: "I travelled to a tropical Pacific island and nearly froze." 😂🇵🇬

full_text: IF YOU VISIT EAST NEW BRITAIN, PAPUA NEW GUINEA, DON’T JUST BOOK A HOTEL ROOM. Book yourself a proper experience. 🇵🇬 One place I’d seriously recommend using as your base is Rapopo Plantation Resort in Kokopo. Because from Rapopo, you’re not limited to sitting beside a swimming pool all day. You can build an entire East New Britain adventure around your stay. Here’s what you can do: 🌊 SWIM AND RELAX BY THE SEA Rapopo sits right along the coastline. You can swim, relax around the resort, sit beside the water, enjoy the pool, watch the sunset or simply do absolutely nothing for an afternoon. Sometimes that’s exactly what a vacation should look like. 🤿 SNORKEL THE WATERS AROUND EAST NEW BRITAIN Grab your mask and get into some of the beautiful tropical waters surrounding the Gazelle Peninsula. Depending on your itinerary, snorkelling trips can take you away from the resort and into reefs and marine environments around the area. 🐬 GO DOLPHIN WATCHING Yes. You can head out early in the morning looking for wild spinner dolphins. Imagine starting your day in Papua New Guinea on a boat, surrounded by tropical islands, watching dolphins cutting through the water. 🐠 SCUBA DIVE If you're a diver, East New Britain gets even more interesting. The area offers reef diving as well as access to WWII-related wreck diving. The waters around Rabaul and Kokopo carry both incredible marine biodiversity and history beneath the surface. ⚓ DIVE WWII WRECKS This is where East New Britain becomes especially interesting for Americans, Australians, Japanese and other visitors interested in Pacific War history. World War II wasn't something that happened somewhere far away from PNG. Some of the fighting happened RIGHT HERE. Today, parts of that history remain underwater. 🌋 EXPLORE RABAUL'S VOLCANIC LANDSCAPE Then get back on land. Head toward Rabaul and explore one of the most dramatic volcanic landscapes in the Pacific. See the Tavurvur area. Look across Simpson Harbour. See the landscape that has repeatedly shaped the history of Rabaul. For someone coming from America, Europe or another part of the world, this isn't your normal resort vacation. 🪖 EXPLORE WWII HISTORY East New Britain is packed with Pacific War history. You can visit: • Japanese tunnels • Wartime relics • Old Rabaul • Historical sites • Museums • Bita Paka War Cemetery • Other locations connected to the Pacific campaign For American visitors whose grandparents or great-grandparents served in the Pacific, this can become much more than tourism. It can become personal. 🏝️ TAKE A BOAT TO THE SURROUNDING ISLANDS You can also leave the mainland. Explore parts of the Duke of York Islands and other islands surrounding the Gazelle Peninsula. Depending on the itinerary, Watom Island and other nearby destinations can also be incorporated. Some of these places receive nowhere near the number of international tourists that comparable tropical islands elsewhere receive. That's part of the appeal. 🎣 GO FISHING Want something quieter? Go fishing. Depending on conditions and arrangements, visitors can organise fishing trips around East New Britain's waters, including deeper-water fishing. 🛶 KAYAK OR CANOE You don't always need a major expedition either. Spend time kayaking, canoeing or simply exploring the coastline around your accommodation. 🌺 WALK THROUGH THE ORCHID GARDEN Rapopo also has an orchid garden where visitors can slow things down and enjoy PNG's tropical vegetation. 💆 GET A SPA TREATMENT After hiking volcanoes, diving, island hopping and exploring Rabaul, this might suddenly become very important. 😂 Take the afternoon off. Get a massage. Eat. Sleep. Start again tomorrow. 🥥 VISIT KOKOPO MARKET Tourism shouldn't only mean staying inside a resort. Go into Kokopo. Walk through the local market. See the produce. See how people live. Talk to Papua New Guineans. Eat local food. Experience normal daily life. That is often where some of the best travel memories come from. 🥁 EXPERIENCE TOLAI CULTURE East New Britain is also home to the Tolai people and some extraordinary cultural traditions. Depending on when you visit, your trip can include traditional performances, cultural experiences, mask traditions and major cultural events. If you happen to travel during one of East New Britain's major festivals, even better. 🦞 EAT FRESH SEAFOOD And obviously… You're sitting beside some of the richest tropical waters in the Pacific. Eat the fish. Eat the lobster. Try local dishes. Enjoy dinner beside the water. 🌅 WATCH THE SUN SET OVER THE WATER Then after everything else… Sit down. Order something cold. Look across the water. And watch another day disappear over Papua New Guinea. This is the side of PNG that much of the world still doesn't know exists. Volcanoes. WWII history. Tropical islands. Dolphins. Scuba diving. Wreck diving. Fishing. Snorkelling. Kayaking. Culture. Markets. Fresh seafood. Beautiful resorts. And some days… Absolutely nothing except the ocean. 🇵🇬 That's why I'm increasingly convinced that places like Rapopo and East New Britain shouldn't be marketed simply as accommodation destinations. They should be sold as complete experiences. I’m building the Visiting PNG side of HausLink around exactly that idea. Not simply: "Here is a hotel." But: "Here is what your entire Papua New Guinea experience could look like." I'm collecting the data, understanding what international travellers actually want, and using that information to build better PNG travel experiences around real demand. And if you know someone who travels internationally looking for destinations that aren't already overrun with tourists… Send this to them. 🇵🇬

full_text: “Australia and New Zealand are re-securitising the Blue Pacific through a parallel, fast-moving architecture of bilateral treaties, defence initiatives and now Forum-endorsed institutions. There are also proposals by the Solomon Islands and the Joint Heads of Pacific Security (JHoPS), seeking permanent legal form in the regional architecture. This is not a future risk to be debated in the abstract. It is already being built, and Leaders convening in Palau for the 55th Pacific Islands Leaders Forum are being asked to formalise it. This is not simply an argument that Australia is imposing a security order on passive Pacific states. The evidence gathered here resists this reading on its own terms: the Pacific Police Support Group’s (PPSG) first deployment operated under Samoan direction and Papua New Guinean operational command, even as external financing and infrastructure remained decisive throughout. The central issue is not whether these initiatives are genuinely Pacific-led or externally driven. Elements of both are present. The problem is the sequence in which the architecture has developed: operational capabilities, financing arrangements and bilateral security commitments have advanced ahead of the regional legal and political framework now being proposed to govern them. The Blue Pacific Ocean of Peace Regional Security Treaty and the Regional Operations Deployment Framework therefore need to be assessed less as new initiatives than as attempts to formalise a security landscape that has already changed. The question that runs through what follows is not simply who is in charge today, but what exactly is being made permanent, under whose authority, and with what limits.”

full_text: AMERICANS ALREADY TRAVEL THOUSANDS OF MILES TO VISIT REMOTE PACIFIC ISLANDS. So why not Papua New Guinea? I’ve been digging into the actual tourism data, because if I’m going to convince more Americans to visit PNG, I need to understand whether the market actually exists. It does. And the numbers are VERY interesting. 🇫🇯 Fiji received approximately 118,148 visitors from the United States in 2025. Think about that for a second. More than ONE HUNDRED THOUSAND Americans flew across the Pacific to visit a small island country thousands of miles from the United States. So the argument that: “Papua New Guinea is simply too far away for Americans” doesn’t really hold up. Distance creates friction. It does NOT eliminate demand. Now look at the Solomon Islands. This is a country that shares far more similarities with Papua New Guinea. - Remote. - Developing infrastructure. - Limited international connectivity. - WWII history. - Diving. - Traditional cultures. - Tropical islands. - Adventure tourism. And in 2024, Americans represented approximately 16.3% of actual tourists visiting the Solomon Islands. They were the SECOND-LARGEST tourist market behind Australia. full_text: To be honest, I’ve been involved in or witnessed some dangerous things in my lifetime. I’ve been in situations where, if not for God’s grace and mercy, I could easily have ended up in jail or in the grave. That’s just the truth. But I’m older now. I have 6 kids. And because of that, the way I look at risk has changed completely. There are parts of London, Melbourne, Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, Baltimore, St. Louis, New Orleans and other major Western cities that I would NOT intentionally walk into at the wrong time of day just to prove a point. Not because I think those cities are terrible. Not because everyone living there is dangerous. But because I understand something very simple: ANYTHING CAN POP OFF. And when you have a wife, children, responsibilities and people depending on you, unnecessary risk stops looking brave and starts looking stupid. The same applies to Papua New Guinea. I’ve been through almost every kind of settlement or ghetto in Port Moresby. Daytime. Night. Early hours of the morning. Under all kinds of circumstances. I still move around different parts of Port Moresby today because business sometimes takes me there. But that familiarity comes from being born here, understanding people, understanding the environment, knowing how to read situations and knowing when something doesn’t feel right. I would NEVER tell a foreign tourist: “I go there all the time, so you’ll be fine.” That would be irresponsible. My experience is not your experience. My familiarity is not your familiarity. And the same logic applies when I travel overseas. Just because millions of people live in London, Chicago, LA or Melbourne does not mean every neighbourhood, every train station, every street and every hour of the night carries the same level of risk. It doesn’t. That is why I keep pushing back against the idea that an ENTIRE COUNTRY should be judged by its most dangerous areas. Papua New Guinea has risky areas. Absolutely. There are places I would not recommend a tourist wander into alone. There are places experiencing tribal conflict. There are situations where poor planning can unnecessarily expose you to crime. But I would apply EXACTLY the same logic in America, the UK, Australia or anywhere else. I’m not taking my children sightseeing through a high-crime neighbourhood at 2AM just because the country has a good international reputation. 😂 Risk is about LOCATION. TIMING. BEHAVIOUR. LOCAL KNOWLEDGE. WHO YOU ARE WITH. AND WHAT IS HAPPENING AROUND YOU. Not simply the name of the country stamped on your passport. And personally, there are parts of the Western world where I would feel more exposed than I would in many parts of Papua New Guinea. That doesn’t make PNG “safer than the West.” That would be an equally foolish generalisation. It simply means risk needs CONTEXT. When I encourage Americans and other foreigners to visit PNG, I am not asking them to switch their brains off. I’m asking them to do the opposite. Plan properly. Use trusted transport. Stay with reputable accommodation providers. Use good guides and tour operators. Listen to local advice. Avoid unnecessary exposure. And enjoy the country intelligently. Because whether you’re in Port Moresby, Chicago, London, Melbourne or Los Angeles… the world is not divided into perfectly safe countries and perfectly dangerous countries. There are safe places. There are risky places. There are good people. There are criminals. And sometimes, anything can pop off. Use common sense. Protect yourself. Protect your family. And don’t let one neighbourhood define an entire nation. But one thing I know for sure, the small towns and countryside locations in the US are the best and probably safest places to visit especially in the Red States.

full_text: I’ve been on X since 2023, so I’ve watched the good, the bad and the downright ugly coming out of America. I’ve seen videos and reports of mass shootings. - Drive-by shootings. - Armed robberies. - Carjackings. - Gang violence. - Drug trafficking. - Human trafficking. - Fentanyl destroying communities. - Home invasions. - Random assaults. - Organized retail theft. - Murders in broad daylight. And some neighborhoods in places like Chicago, Baltimore, Memphis, St. Louis, New Orleans, Philadelphia, Los Angeles and New York have serious crime problems. But here’s the thing. I would NEVER look at one dangerous neighborhood in an American city and conclude: “America is unsafe. Never go there.” That would be ridiculous. America is enormous. It has some of the most beautiful places on Earth. - The Grand Canyon. - Yellowstone. - Alaska. - Hawaii. - The Rocky Mountains. - Florida’s beaches. - The Texas countryside. - California’s coastline. - The Great Smoky Mountains. - New England. - Small-town America. - The Pacific Northwest. And thousands of communities where ordinary people are simply raising families, working, running businesses, going to church, eating good food and living normal lives. Then there’s the FOOD. - Texas barbecue. - Louisiana Cajun and Creole food. - New York pizza. - Southern cooking. - Steaks. - Seafood. - Burgers. - Mexican-American cuisine. - Hawaiian food. And almost every international cuisine imaginable because America has people from practically everywhere. That is the perspective I want Americans to have when looking at Papua New Guinea. 🇵🇬 Yes, PNG has problems. I’m not going to lie to you about them. There are areas with crime. There are places affected by tribal fighting. There are communities where you need local knowledge, proper transportation and coordination. There are places I would NOT recommend a foreign visitor wander into without guidance. But that is NOT the whole country. Just like the worst parts of Baltimore, Chicago, LA or any other American city do not represent the United States. You don’t commonly associate PNG with the kinds of mass shootings, school shootings, interstate drive-bys, large-scale gang shootouts or fentanyl epidemics Americans regularly hear about at home. Our risks are different. And they need to be managed differently. But beyond those risks is an extraordinary country. - Tropical islands. - White-sand beaches. - Coral reefs. - Volcanoes. - Fjords. - Mountain ranges. - Rainforests.- Birds of Paradise. - Thousands of plant and animal species. - More than 800 languages. - Hundreds of cultures. - Traditional villages. - WWII history connecting PNG directly to America. - Some of the best diving in the Pacific. - Fishing. - Surfing. - Hiking. - Birdwatching. - Cultural festivals. - Fresh seafood. - Mumu. - Tropical fruits. And some of the most welcoming communities you will ever experience. That’s the PNG I’m trying to introduce to Americans. Not by pretending our problems don’t exist. But by putting them into perspective. When you travel anywhere in the world, you research where you are going. You choose where you stay. You understand which areas to avoid. You use reputable operators. You listen to local advice. You plan properly. PNG should be treated the same way. Don’t judge 10 million+ people and an entire country from one headline, one crime story, one old documentary or one travel warning. You wouldn’t want me judging America that way. So while I continue promoting Papua New Guinea to my American audience, that’s all I ask: VIEW PNG WITH THE SAME PERSPECTIVE YOU VIEW YOUR OWN COUNTRY. full_text: Rarely does Western media give adequate coverage to issues of grave concern in Indonesia-occupied West Papua. Read on: Peaceful Protest of the Melanesian People of West Papua Rejecting Militarism and the Spaceport in Biak A number of photos we received today carry a strong message from the Melanesian people of West Papua in Biak. Through a peaceful action, the community firmly and openly expressed its rejection to the Government of Indonesia regarding militarization programs and the plan to build a Spaceport on Biak Island. This peaceful protest was joined by the Melanesian people of West Papua and led directly by church and customary leaders, namely Rev. John Baransano as a representative of the Evangelical Christian Church in the Land of Papua, and Apolos Sroyer as a customary leader of the Biak community. The presence of spiritual and traditional leaders shows that this struggle is not the interest of a particular group, but the collective voice of the Biak people who seek to defend their land, sea, and living space. In the action, the people emphasized that Biak is not an empty territory for military interests and strategic projects without the consent of Indigenous peoples. The land of Papua is a land of life, not a weapons testing ground, nor a space for exploitation that ignores the rights of Indigenous Papuans. The Melanesian people of West Papua demand that the government stop its militaristic approach and open space for honest, fair, and dignified dialogue with the Indigenous people of Biak. Development must be based on the consent of the people, respect customary land rights, protect the environment, and guarantee the future of Papuan generations, rather than bringing fear and new conflict. This peaceful action sends a message that the people of Papua are not silent. They stand with dignity, voicing justice, peace, and the right to determine the future of their own land. - from the West Papuan Human Rights centre.

full_text: 🚨 CHINA’S PACIFIC MISSILE TEST RAISES TENSIONS WITH AUSTRALIA. SYDNEY, AUSTRALIA - China’s recent test of a long‑range ballistic missile in the South Pacific has sharpened concerns in Australia over Beijing’s expanding military reach across a region both countries are courting. The missile, launched in early July from a Chinese nuclear submarine, traveled thousands of kilometers before splashing down south of Kiribati, a remote island nation that has become strategically relevant as major powers compete for influence. Australian officials said they received only brief advance notice, describing the test as part of a pattern of increasingly assertive Chinese military activity. The launch followed a similar long‑range test last year that landed near French Polynesia and marked another departure from China’s earlier practice of conducting missile trials within its own territory. Kiribati’s location has drawn growing attention as China deepens security and infrastructure ties across the Pacific. The island chain sits near key maritime routes and within reach of U.S. bases in Hawaii and Guam. Australia has stepped up its own engagement, signing new defense agreements with Fiji and expanding cooperation with Papua New Guinea and other Pacific states. Analysts say the missile was likely a JL‑3, China’s newest submarine‑launched system capable of reaching intercontinental ranges. Before the test, China positioned tracking vessels near Guam, suggesting a rehearsal of operations far from its coastline. Pacific governments reacted unevenly. Australia, Japan, New Zealand and the United States criticized the launch, while several island nations expressed unease but stopped short of a unified response. full_text: AMERICA JUST CELEBRATED 250 YEARS OF INDEPENDENCE. 🇺🇸 Fireworks. History. The Declaration of Independence. National symbols. Stories about how a country came to be. Now here's an interesting piece of Papua New Guinea's own economic history. Our modern currency is literally named after traditional shell wealth. 🇵🇬 The currency you use in PNG today is the: KINA. And its smaller unit is the: TOEA. Those aren't random names invented by economists. They come from shells historically used for trade, wealth and ceremonial exchange in Papua New Guinea. The Bank of PNG specifically traces both names to traditional shell currencies. Bank of PNG But it gets more interesting. Among the Tolai people of East New Britain there is another traditional shell money called: TABU. And unlike something sitting behind glass in a museum... tabu is still culturally alive. It remains important in customary obligations, funerals, bride price, wealth distribution and other transactions in Tolai society. Recent PNG reporting describes it continuing to circulate alongside modern money in parts of the Gazelle Peninsula. Imagine visiting Kokopo or Rabaul... pulling modern kina notes from your wallet... and then meeting people whose families still understand an entirely different system of wealth that predates the national currency. That's the part of PNG I'd like international visitors to experience. Not simply: - Hotel. - Beach. - Airport. - Home. But moments when you suddenly realize: “These people have an entire economic and cultural system I knew absolutely nothing about.” America is 250 years into its national story. Papua New Guinea became independent only in 1975. But many of the cultures contained inside PNG carry systems, customs and histories extending far beyond the modern state. That distinction matters. PNG may be a relatively young country. Its cultures are not. And sometimes the best reason to travel somewhere is discovering how much you didn't know. 🇺🇸🤝🇵🇬

She became one of the most famous American anthropologists of the 20th century. But part of her story runs straight through Papua New Guinea. Mead conducted fieldwork in the Admiralty Islands/Manus in 1928–1929, and later worked among New Guinea communities including the Arapesh, Mundugumor and Tchambuli during fieldwork in the early 1930s. Her papers documenting that work are now held by the U.S. Library of Congress. Stop and think about that. An American woman travelled across the Pacific almost a century ago... into communities in this part of the world... and spent years trying to understand how people raised children, organized families, exchanged goods, formed relationships and understood society. Her work became part of major debates inside American anthropology. And yet today, many Americans probably couldn't point to Papua New Guinea on a map. That's what fascinates me. PNG has crossed paths with American history, scholarship, warfare, exploration, science and culture far more than most people realize. The connections exist. We've simply done a terrible job telling the stories. So if you're American and you're reading all these PNG posts from me thinking: “Why would I ever go there?” Maybe start with curiosity. Look up Manus. Look up Margaret Mead. Look up the Sepik. Look up New Ireland. Look up the Highlands. Then keep going. You may discover that Papua New Guinea is not nearly as disconnected from the world you know as you assumed. And perhaps one day instead of reading about it... you'll come see it yourself. 🇺🇸🤝🇵🇬

full_text: If you’re an American looking for a destination that feels genuinely different from the usual international travel circuit, Rabaul in East New Britain should be on your list for one simple reason: nowhere else gives you such a powerful combination of World War II history, active volcanic landscapes, island culture, and raw Pacific scenery in one compact place. Rabaul is not just another tropical destination. It is a place where history is still physically embedded in the land and ocean. During World War II, Rabaul became one of Japan’s most important military bases in the South Pacific. Thousands of troops were stationed there, tunnels were carved into hillsides, aircraft operated from nearby airfields, and the surrounding waters became part of a much larger battle for control of the Pacific. For Americans, that history is not distant. It is connected directly to the sacrifices made by U.S. servicemen across the Pacific campaign. Today, you can stand in places where that history happened. You can explore old Japanese tunnels, coastal defenses, war relics and sites that once formed part of an enormous military network. Then, within the same journey, you can look across Simpson Harbour toward volcanic peaks that completely changed the city’s story decades later. That is what makes Rabaul unique. This is not a museum where history sits behind glass. The entire landscape tells the story. Mount Tavurvur remains one of the most recognizable features of the area. The 1994 volcanic eruptions devastated large parts of old Rabaul, covering sections of the town in ash and forcing many businesses and residents to relocate toward Kokopo. Yet Rabaul survived. That creates a travel experience with layers. You are not only visiting a beautiful Pacific island. You are walking through a place shaped by war, rebuilt after destruction, surrounded by volcanoes, coral seas, traditional communities and some of the most dramatic scenery in Papua New Guinea. For American travelers who enjoy history, military heritage, photography, adventure, diving or destinations with a real story behind them, Rabaul offers something completely different from Hawaii, Fiji or the Caribbean. And that is exactly the point. Papua New Guinea is not competing by being more familiar. Its strength is that it still feels undiscovered. A trip to Rabaul can include visits to war sites, volcanic viewpoints, local markets, cultural performances, island excursions, snorkeling, diving, dolphin watching, seafood, village experiences and time along the coast around Kokopo and the Gazelle Peninsula. But the strongest reason to come is the feeling of standing somewhere that connects America’s Pacific history with one of the most extraordinary landscapes on Earth. If you ever visit Papua New Guinea, do not just pass through Port Moresby. Put Rabaul on the itinerary. You may arrive because of the history. You will probably leave remembering the people, the volcanoes, the ocean and the feeling that you discovered somewhere most Americans still know almost nothing about. Register your interest here: https://t.co/uA0lzRPJAq For travelers tired of predictable destinations, that rarity alone makes Rabaul worth crossing the Pacific to experience at least once personally.
